objectives.understand: How Role, Context and Format (R-C-F) shape an answer, and why AI can state false things confidently.
objectives.do: Rewrite a one-line request as an R-C-F prompt and run the 4-question check on an answer.
objectives.demonstrate: Diagnose weak prompts, classify what is safe to paste, and judge whether a claim is verified.
objectives.apply: Produce one R-C-F rewrite and one written verification record from your own field.

discover.title: Mission briefing: the confident number
discover.scenario: A colleague in Abuja pastes an AI answer into a draft for the Permanent Secretary: '68.4% of Nigerian adults are banked, according to the 2023 CBN Inclusion Report.' It sounds precise. Is the report real? Is the year right? Is 68.4% even the right definition of 'banked'? Today you learn to ask better questions and to catch a confident guess before it carries your name.

keyIdeas: R-C-F: give the AI a Role, the Context (your real material) and the Format you want.
AI produces confident guesses. The more specific a number or citation, the more you must verify it.
Run the 4-question check: source named? source exists? numbers add up? would you sign it?

missions.title: Label the R-C-F parts
missions.scenario: A teacher in Kano wrote this prompt to get a letter to parents about a change to exam dates.
missions.prompt: Sort each line of her prompt into Role, Context or Format.

items.text: You are the head teacher of a Nigerian secondary school.
items.feedback: This sets who the AI should be, so it is the Role.

items.text: The JSS3 exams move from 3 June to 10 June because the hall is being repaired.
items.feedback: This is the situation itself, so it is Context.

items.text: The letter goes to parents, many of whom read English as a second language.
items.feedback: Who the reader is belongs to Context. It changes the words the AI chooses.

items.text: Under 150 words, warm tone, with the new date in bold in the first line.
items.feedback: Length, tone and layout are the shape of the answer, so this is Format.

items.text: End with one line telling parents who to call with questions.
items.feedback: This describes how the letter should be structured, so it is Format.

missions.hint: Role = who the AI is. Context = the situation and the reader. Format = the shape of the answer.
missions.support: Ask of each line: does it describe the writer (Role), the facts and the audience (Context), or what the finished letter should look like (Format)?
missions.explain: With all three in place the AI writes like a head teacher, uses the real dates and reasons, and produces a short, warm letter with the key fact up front. Missing any one of them is how you get a generic answer.

missions.title: Check the confident number
missions.scenario: The AI told your colleague: '68.4% of Nigerian adults are banked, according to the 2023 CBN Inclusion Report.'
missions.prompt: What should go into the draft for the Permanent Secretary?

options.text: Use it. It names a specific report and a precise figure, so it is probably right.
options.feedback: Precision is not proof. Invented citations look exactly like this. 'Does the source exist?' is the question that catches them.

options.text: Search for the report on the CBN or EFInA website. Only use the figure if you find it, with its year and definition, and cite the original publication.
options.feedback: Correct. You check that the source exists, that it says what the AI claims, and what the figure actually measures.

options.text: Ask the AI 'Are you sure?' and use the figure if it says yes.
options.feedback: The AI will often confirm its own guess. Asking the same tool again is not verification. Go to the original source.

options.text: Delete all statistics from the draft so nothing can be wrong.
options.feedback: Safe, but it throws away useful evidence. The skill is to verify the number, not avoid numbers.

missions.hint: Which of the four check questions is this about? Two of them deal with sources.
missions.support: Imagine the Permanent Secretary asks 'where is this from?' The only good answer is the original document, opened and read by you. The AI's say-so isn't enough.
missions.explain: You trust the structure and verify the facts. A named source must exist and must say what the AI claims, for the stated year and definition. Then the figure can carry your name.

advanced.title: Advanced: the privacy card
advanced.scenario: You are about to paste material into a free AI tool. Decide what is safe as it is, what needs anonymising first, and what never goes in.

items.text: A published federal ministry policy document
items.feedback: Public documents are safe to paste.

items.text: Your own rough notes from a staff meeting
items.feedback: Your own notes are fine once you take out names and anything confidential.

items.text: The office payroll sheet with names and salaries
items.feedback: Salaries and payroll never go into a free AI tool, anonymised or not.

items.text: Customer complaints that include phone numbers
items.feedback: The complaints are useful, but strip the phone numbers and names first.

items.text: A contract marked confidential that has not been signed
items.feedback: Anything marked confidential or unpublished stays out of free tools.

items.text: A public news article about your industry
items.feedback: Public information is safe to paste.

advanced.hint: Ask: is it already public? Does it identify a person? Is it marked confidential or about pay?
advanced.support: Picture pinning the text on a public notice board. If that's fine, paste it. If it would be fine once names were removed, anonymise it first. If it must never be seen, it never goes in.
advanced.explain: You are sending text to another company's computers. Public material is fine, your own material needs anonymising, and payroll, confidential or unpublished documents never go in.
